ux-design-agency-dubai.problemHeading: What working in the UAE actually requires

problems.name: Arabic is not a translation task
problems.body: RTL mirrors layout, but numerals stay left-to-right, directional icons each need a decision, and the visual centre of gravity shifts. A mirrored English site is instantly recognisable to a native reader — and in a trust-driven purchase, that is disqualifying.

problems.name: The audience is genuinely multilingual
problems.body: A Dubai product may serve Emirati, South Asian, European and Chinese users in one session mix. Designing for a single assumed reader — in either direction — quietly excludes a large part of the market.

problems.name: Regulated finance has its own perimeter
problems.body: DIFC and ADGM operate distinct regulatory regimes with their own onboarding and disclosure expectations. Fintech flows built for an Indian or US regime need genuine rework, not relabelling.

problems.name: Premium is the baseline, not the aspiration
problems.body: In Dubai's property and luxury segments, competitors are already presenting at a high standard. Adequate design reads as a downgrade rather than as neutral.

deliverables.name: Arabic RTL design
deliverables.body: Genuine bidirectional design — layout, numerals, iconography, typography and reading gravity handled correctly rather than flipped with a stylesheet flag.

deliverables.name: Luxury property experiences
deliverables.body: Immersive project sites and qualification journeys for developers and brokerages, built on the system behind seven Dubai properties.

deliverables.name: Regulated fintech flows
deliverables.body: Onboarding, KYC and payment journeys designed around DIFC and ADGM expectations, worked through with your compliance team rather than around them.

deliverables.name: Multi-market design systems
deliverables.body: One system serving Arabic and English without maintaining two parallel design efforts — the difference between a manageable product and a doubling of cost.

deliverables.name: Enterprise and government-adjacent standards
deliverables.body: WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility and the documentation standards that surface in UAE enterprise and semi-government procurement.

deliverables.name: Same-day collaboration
deliverables.body: India to Gulf is a 1.5-hour offset. Full working-day overlap, live calls at normal hours, and no waiting overnight for an answer.

process.name: Market and language scoping
process.body: Week 1. Which languages, which audiences, which regulatory perimeter. Getting this wrong is the most expensive mistake available in a UAE project.

process.name: Structure
process.body: Weeks 2–3. Architecture and flows designed bidirectionally from the start, because retrofitting RTL is substantially more expensive than designing for it.

process.name: Design
process.body: Weeks 3–8. Visual design in both directions, reviewed against the standard the local competitive set is already setting.

process.name: Handover
process.body: Ongoing. Specs covering both language directions, with the RTL rules documented so your engineers are not guessing.

proof.title: Rcentric — seven Dubai properties

proof.related: See the Rcentric case study, our PropTech practice, and our guide to Arabic RTL design.

pricing.title: How UAE engagements run
pricing.body: Quoted in USD or AED. Bilingual projects carry genuine additional scope — roughly a third more design work than a single-direction equivalent — and we scope for that upfront rather than raising it midway. See the pricing page.
pricing.timeline: A single property experience runs 6–8 weeks; bilingual product work is typically 10–12.

faqs.q: Do you have actual UAE experience, or just a Dubai landing page?
faqs.a: Actual experience. We designed seven luxury property experiences in Dubai through Rcentric, including work for Omniyat, with a 3x increase in qualified leads across the portfolio. That is the only UAE claim we make — we are an India-based studio serving UAE clients, not a Dubai-registered agency, and we would rather say that plainly than imply a local office we do not have.

faqs.q: How do you handle Arabic RTL properly?
faqs.a: By designing bidirectionally from the start rather than mirroring at the end. Layout flips, but numerals remain left-to-right, directional icons each need an individual decision, Arabic typography has different vertical rhythm and line-height needs, and the visual entry point of every screen moves. We document these rules in handover so engineering is not making judgement calls.

faqs.q: Can you work with DIFC or ADGM-regulated entities?
faqs.a: Yes. Both operate distinct regulatory regimes with their own onboarding, disclosure and record-keeping expectations, so fintech flows designed for another jurisdiction need genuine rework rather than relabelling. We work directly with your compliance team from week one, because designing first and seeking approval later is how these projects overrun.

faqs.q: What are your working hours relative to the UAE?
faqs.a: India is 1.5 hours ahead of Gulf Standard Time, so we share essentially the entire working day. Live calls happen at normal hours for both sides, and you are not waiting overnight for a response — which is the practical difference between a Gulf-adjacent partner and a US or European one.

faqs.q: Do you work in Abu Dhabi and the wider Gulf as well as Dubai?
faqs.a: Yes. Our delivered work is concentrated in Dubai, but the design considerations — bilingual audiences, RTL, premium expectations, Gulf regulatory context — carry across Abu Dhabi, Saudi Arabia and the wider GCC. Market-specific conventions differ and we scope for that.

faqs.q: Can you handle both English and Arabic in one design system?
faqs.a: That is the efficient approach and what we recommend. A single bidirectional system with direction-aware tokens and components costs meaningfully less to build and far less to maintain than two parallel design efforts, and it prevents the two language versions drifting apart over time.

ui-ux-design-agency-usa.problemHeading: What US software teams tend to need

problems.name: Accessibility is a litigation surface
problems.body: ADA web accessibility claims in the US run into the thousands annually, and enterprise procurement increasingly requires a VPAT. Designing to WCAG 2.1 AA from the start costs a fraction of retrofitting under legal pressure.

problems.name: In-house senior design is expensive and slow to hire
problems.body: A senior product designer in a US metro is a significant salary plus a months-long search. For many teams the constraint is not budget in principle — it is getting senior capacity onto the problem this quarter.

problems.name: Enterprise buyers audit design maturity
problems.body: Procurement reviews now examine accessibility conformance, design consistency and documentation. Inconsistency that a startup tolerates internally becomes a blocker in an enterprise sales cycle.

problems.name: Offshore has burned you before
problems.body: The common failure is not skill — it is layers. Account managers relaying requirements, junior designers appearing after the pitch, and no overlap hours. Those are structural choices, and we have made the opposite ones.

deliverables.name: Senior designers, directly
deliverables.body: No account managers and no junior hand-off after the sale. You work with the people designing your product, which is the main reason clients move to retainers with us.

deliverables.name: ADA and WCAG 2.1 AA compliance
deliverables.body: Contrast, keyboard navigation, focus states and screen-reader semantics designed in rather than retrofitted — with the documentation enterprise procurement asks for.

deliverables.name: SaaS product design
deliverables.body: Dashboards, onboarding and workflow tools — the surfaces where usability drives activation and retention. See our SaaS product design service.

deliverables.name: Async-first collaboration
deliverables.body: Loom walkthroughs, structured written updates and Figma comments, so progress does not depend on both sides being awake simultaneously — with EST/PST overlap for the conversations that genuinely need it.

deliverables.name: US contracting norms
deliverables.body: USD contracts, NDAs and IP assignment as standard, with W-8BEN documentation handled so your finance team is not solving an unfamiliar problem.

deliverables.name: Engineering-compatible handover
deliverables.body: Specs designed against your stack and sprint cadence, delivered in increments matching your release rhythm rather than one large drop at the end.

pricing.body: Project, retainer or fixed-scope audit, quoted and contracted in USD. Most US clients start with a two-week UX audit because it is the lowest-risk way to test working together across a distance. See the pricing page.
pricing.timeline: Design kickoff within 48 hours of signature. Focused work runs 3–5 weeks; a full product redesign with a design system is 10–12.

faqs.q: How do you handle the time difference with US teams?
faqs.a: We keep a 9am–1pm EST overlap window for live calls and reviews, and run everything else async — Loom walkthroughs, written updates, Figma comments. In practice most US clients find this faster than a local agency, because async forces decisions to be written down rather than lost in a meeting. For PST teams the overlap shifts earlier in our day.

faqs.q: Do you have a US office?
faqs.a: No. We are an India-based studio serving US clients remotely, and we would rather state that plainly than imply a presence we do not have. What we do offer is USD contracting, US-standard NDAs and IP assignment, EST/PST overlap hours, and senior designers on your project rather than an account layer.

faqs.q: Do you design to ADA and WCAG standards?
faqs.a: WCAG 2.1 AA is our default, not an upgrade. In the US this matters commercially as well as ethically — web accessibility claims run into the thousands annually and enterprise procurement increasingly requires a VPAT. Designing to standard from the start costs a fraction of retrofitting under legal pressure.

faqs.q: How do you handle IP, NDAs and contracting?
faqs.a: US-standard NDAs, full IP assignment on payment, and USD contracts. We provide W-8BEN documentation so your finance team is not navigating an unfamiliar process. These are routine for us — most of our client base is outside India.

faqs.q: Why work with an India-based studio rather than a US agency?
faqs.a: The honest answer is cost and senior availability. You get senior designers directly rather than the account-manager-plus-junior structure common at that price point in the US, and capacity is available in weeks rather than after a months-long hire. The real trade-off is timezone, which async working and a defined overlap window address but do not eliminate — if you need someone in the room daily, hire locally.

Design kickoff is normally within 48 hours of signature. We run a structured onboarding session to gather product context, access and analytics, and typically have an initial direction within five working days.
